orders.description: Bronx County order entered July 13, 2012, on East 163rd LLC’s motion
orders.trial_court_action: Denied East 163rd LLC’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Gautier alleged that he slipped on a wet substance on a stairway in defendant’s apartment building. The opinion does not identify the substance.

legal_issues.finding: East 163rd argued it had not created the hazard. The majority decided the motion on constructive notice.
East 163rd denied actual notice. The majority made no separate finding on that issue.
The superintendent described a janitorial schedule, but East 163rd did not establish compliance on the accident date or when the stairway was last inspected. Constructive notice remained disputed.

evidence_discussed.description: East 163rd submitted its superintendent’s deposition on the regular janitorial schedule.

quality.notes: The caretaker’s logbook, bottle and earlier inspections discussed in the comparisons belong to cited cases. The majority’s affirmance controls.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Julia I. Rodriguez, J.), entered July 13, 2012, which denied defendant East 163rd LLC’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it, affirmed, without costs.
Plaintiff alleges that he slipped and fell on a wet substance that was on the stairway of defendant’s apartment building.
Defendant moved for summary judgment on the ground that it did not create or have actual or constructive notice of the hazard.
In support of the motion, defendant submitted the deposition testimony of its superintendent about the building’s regular janitorial schedule.
However, it offered no evidence that the schedule was followed on the day of the accident
Moreover, constructive notice remains an issue in this case because defendant made no showing as to when the stairway was last inspected before plaintiffs accident
Defendant’s proof that a janitorial schedule merely existed does not suffice for purposes of showing that it was followed.

This admission involved the critical question of the condition of the premises within a reasonable time before the accident — a question the moving defendants did not address in this case, Williams or Aviles .

orders.description: Kings County order dated December 27, 2017, insofar as appealed from
orders.trial_court_action: Granted both the garage owner’s and snow-removal contractor’s motions for summary judgment dismissing the claims against them.

facts.factual_summary: Pennino alleged that he slipped on snow and ice at about 8 p.m. on February 13, 2014, in a parking garage open to the elements on three sides. Plaza owned the garage and hired Universal for snow and ice removal.

legal_issues.finding: A temporary lull did not trigger a duty to clear snow or ice before the storm ended.
The meteorological evidence established that the storm continued through the accident. Pennino did not raise a triable issue that it had ended or that the ice predated it.
Pennino failed to raise a triable issue that the ice on which he fell had existed before the storm.
The court credited the meteorologists’ affidavits concerning the storm’s duration; the weather evidence was consistent with Pennino’s testimony.

evidence_discussed.description: Meteorologists’ affidavits addressed the duration and severity of the winter storm.
Climatological evidence described a rain or drizzle interval followed by further snow accumulation; the court also noted a regional storm warning.
Pennino testified it was snowing when he entered the ambulance after the fall.

quality.notes: The court affirmed one appealed order covering both defendants. A separate contractor-duty ruling is not stated.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Larry D. Martin, J.), dated December 27, 2017. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the defendants' separate motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with one bill of costs.
The plaintiff alleges that on February 13, 2014, at approximately 8:00 p.m., he slipped and fell on snow and ice in a parking garage, which was exposed to the elements on three sides.

The parking garage was owned by the defendant Brooklyn Kings Plaza, LLC (hereinafter Plaza). Plaza hired the defendant Universal Allied Services, Inc. (hereinafter Universal), to perform snow and ice removal services.

The defendants separately moved, inter alia, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them, arguing, among other things, that the plaintiff's fall occurred during an ongoing winter storm, before the duty to clear the premises arose.
A lull in the storm does not impose a duty to remove the accumulation of snow or ice before the storm ceases in its entirety

The defendants demonstrated, through the affidavits of expert meteorologists and other evidence, that a winter storm producing snow, other wintry precipitation, and blizzard-like conditions began in the early morning hours of February 13, 2014, and continued until the morning of February 14, 2014.
Indeed, on February 13, Governor Andrew Cuomo declared a State Disaster Emergency, and a winter storm warning was issued for the tri-state area continuing until 6:00 a.m. on February 14, 2014.
Although there was a lull in the storm on February 13, during which there was only rain, light rain, or drizzle recorded, the winter weather resumed and a further accumulation of snow occurred
the expert and climatological evidence submitted by the defendants was consistent with the plaintiff's testimony at his deposition that it was snowing when he got into the ambulance after his fall.
Accordingly, the defendants demonstrated, prima facie, that the plaintiff's accident occurred during an ongoing storm

In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact either as to whether the storm had ceased at the time of the accident or whether the ice condition on which the plaintiff fell existed prior to the storm on February 13

Therefore, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to grant those branches of the defendants' separate motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Sermos tripped on a loose board of the backyard deck at defendants’ home and fell into the attached pool. Two boards had been removed for a pool-light repair and left unsecured. No one witnessed the accident.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants failed to warn of the latent danger created by the unsecured boards.
Defendants’ admissions supported the conclusion that they created the loose-board condition during the repair.
Plaintiffs established that the loose boards proximately caused the injuries. Defendants offered no admissible evidence raising a genuine competing account.
The hospital notations about jumping were unattributed and unrelated to diagnosis or treatment. They were inadmissible for their truth and did not raise a triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiffs relied on defendants’ admissions concerning the loose deck boards after all parties were deposed.
Defendants offered uncertified medical records containing a competing account; the court upheld exclusion of the records.

quality.notes: The order established liability for the deck trip. The excluded hospital account of jumping into the pool is not an established accident fact.

evidence.quote: the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Eastoressa, J.), dated May 11, 2011, which granted the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff Glenn Sermos (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) tripped and fell on a loose board of the backyard deck at the defendants’ home, causing him to fall into the attached pool and sustain injuries. There were no witnesses to the accident.

It was later discovered that the defendant Eietro Gruppuso had been attempting to repair a pool light earlier in the day, which required him to remove two wooden boards from the attached deck, and that he failed to secure them back in place afterwards, leaving them loose and unstable.

Following discovery, which included the dep *986 ositions of all parties, the plaintiffs moved for summary judgment on the issue of liability, relying primarily on the admissions of the defendants regarding the loose boards on the backyard deck.

The defendants opposed the motion, submitting and relying primarily on certain notes contained in uncertified medical records of the injured plaintiff which state, in part, that he was injured while jumping into the pool.
We affirm.

Here, the plaintiffs met their burden on their motion for summary judgment by submitting evidence that the defendants created the defective and dangerous condition that was the proximate cause of the injured plaintiffs injuries
and failed to warn of the latent dangerous condition

The Supreme Court correctly concluded that the defendants failed to tender admissible evidence sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact as to the proximate cause of the injured plaintiffs injuries.
Initially, we observe that the notations in the hospital record upon which the defendants rely were not attributed to the injured plaintiff.
none of these notations was germane to his diagnosis or treatment and, at trial, would *987 not be admissible for their truth under the business records exception to the hearsay rule

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly excluded the medical records from its consideration, and properly held that the defendants failed to raise a triable issue of fact in opposition to the plaintiffs’ motion

orders.description: Kings County order dated October 4, 2019, insofar as appealed from
orders.trial_court_action: Denied All Jersey’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Uziel allegedly slipped while shopping in the cleaning-products aisle of a Target store. After the fall she saw bleach on the floor. All Jersey provided overnight cleaning and daytime porters on a schedule set by Target.

legal_issues.finding: The contract alone did not create a duty to a shopper, but negligent performance that launched a force or instrument of harm could give rise to liability.
All Jersey failed to rule out its porters’ creation of the hazard. The court did not find that a porter spilled the bleach.
Uziel alleged creation, bringing the affirmative-harm exception into issue. All Jersey supplied no evidence of its porters’ day-of-accident services to negate that exception.
All Jersey’s initial showing was insufficient, so the opposing papers did not need to be assessed.

evidence_discussed.description: Deposition testimony described the arrangement for overnight cleaning and ad hoc daytime porters.

quality.notes: The appeal concerned the shopper’s direct negligence claim against the contractor. No day-specific janitorial evidence was submitted.

evidence.quote: the defendant All Jersey Janitorial Service NY, Inc., appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Devin P. Cohen, J.), dated October 4, 2019. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that branch of that defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly sustained personal injuries when she slipped and fell while shopping in the cleaning products aisle of a Target department store.
After falling, the plaintiff observed that the floor was wet with bleach.

The deposition testimony of various witnesses indicated that the defendant All Jersey Janitorial Service NY, Inc. (hereinafter All Jersey), contracted with the defendant Target Corporation (hereinafter Target) to provide overnight janitorial and cleaning services, and to provide daytime porters to Target on an ad hoc basis on a schedule determined by Target.
The plaintiff commenced this action against the defendants alleging, inter alia, that they had negligently created the dangerous condition.
The Supreme Court denied All Jersey's motion, concluding, among other things, that there were triable issues of fact as to whether All Jersey created the dangerous condition.
All Jersey appeals, and we affirm insofar as appealed from.
Generally, a contractual obligation, standing alone, will not give rise to tort liability in favor of a third party

the Court of Appeals has recognized an exception to this general rule where the contracting party, in failing to exercise reasonable care in the performance of its duties, launches a force or instrument of harm

a contracting defendant is only required to negate the applicability of those Espinal exceptions that were expressly pleaded by the plaintiff or expressly set forth in the plaintiff's bill of particulars

it failed to affirmatively demonstrate, prima facie, that its daytime porters did not launch a force or instrument of harm, as it submitted no evidence regarding the janitorial services provided by All Jersey on the day of the accident

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied All Jersey's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it, without regard to the sufficiency of the opposing papers

orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Peralta-Mejia, a resident of the apartment building owned and managed by defendants, alleged that he slipped on water on the lobby floor.

legal_issues.finding: Owners were not required to mat every floor or continuously mop tracked-in moisture. Creation or notice with time to remedy could support liability.
Defendants established prima facie that they did not create the water condition.
Defendants demonstrated lack of actual notice; the plaintiff raised no triable issue.
Defendants likewise established lack of constructive notice on the record described.

quality.notes: The opinion identifies residence but does not specify a lease. It discusses tracked-in precipitation as a legal standard without identifying the precise source of this water or a particular inspection.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Salvatore Modica, J.), dated June 18, 2019. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff, who lived in an apartment building owned and managed by the defendants, allegedly sustained personal injuries when he slipped and fell on water on the floor of the lobby of that building.
While a defendant is not required to cover all of its floors with mats, or to continuously mop up all moisture resulting from tracked-in precipitation

a defendant may be held liable for an injury proximately caused by a dangerous condition created by water, snow, or ice tracked into a building if it either created the hazardous condition, or had actual or constructive notice of the condition and a reasonable time to undertake remedial action

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition or have actual or constructive notice of its existence
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
